answer.summary: Don’t treat all negative feedback as evidence that a rewrite is wrong: users may be upset simply because a familiar setup changed. Separate that reaction from feedback identifying genuine problems, and account for whether the rewrite was implemented well enough to evaluate.

sections.heading: Separate disruption from product failure
sections.content: Gustav warned that teams can mistake users’ discomfort with a changed, familiar experience for proof the redesign was bad. He compared it to rearranging someone’s desk after they had used the same setup for years: even if the new arrangement is objectively better, the person may initially be less effective and upset. Teams should distinguish that reaction from users being upset because the product actually failed to solve their needs. He cited Facebook’s move to a single News Feed as an example of a change that upset people but solved user problems.

sections.heading: Don’t misread an incomplete rewrite as a failed idea
sections.content: He also cautioned that a major rewrite can produce a false negative if too many pieces must be in place before the underlying hypothesis can be evaluated. For example, a new feed might seem like the wrong idea when the real issue is that its interface or machine learning is poor; teams may need substantial implementation before they can tell.
